summary: The root cause is a redis-cache internal primary failure: redis-cache-2 failed three consecutive PING health checks at 13:22:10Z and the platform promoted replica redis-cache-3, whose dataset was explicitly EMPTY because it was still resyncing (13:22:52Z, F34). That emptied the shared cache, forcing market-data-service to rebuild nearly every quote from the exchange feed snapshot (1-7s per request, F28); with request volume unchanged (F25/F26) this extra per-request work drove market-data-service CPU from ~45% to ~90% (F14) and its p99 from ~40ms to ~1.9s (F10/F15), which pricing-engine then hit synchronously, breaching its deadline and pushing p99 >2s up through api-gateway to the trading screens (F7/F9/F11). All competing hypotheses are contradicted by direct telemetry: market-data request_rate is flat at onset (F25/F26), pricing-engine CPU is unsaturated (F12), exchange-gateway latency is flat (F16), redis evictions did not spike (F31), and no deployment or config change preceded onset (F1/F2/F3/F19-F22). Confidence is medium (0.72), capped because the miss-storm→CPU-saturation hop is inferred from co-timing plus log text rather than a controlled pre/post comparison, and the sub-cause of redis-cache-2's PING failure is not captured by any telemetry.

ranked_hypotheses.title: redis-cache internal primary failure -> empty-replica failover -> cache-miss storm -> market-data-service CPU saturation -> pricing-engine deadline breaches
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The redis-cache primary node (redis-cache-2) failed health checks (3 consecutive PING timeouts) and was marked down at 13:22:10Z; the platform promoted replica redis-cache-3, whose dataset was EMPTY because it was still resyncing (13:22:52Z). That emptied the shared cache. market-data-service, a redis-cache consumer, then had to rebuild nearly every quote from the exchange feed snapshot ('cache miss storm: quote:<n> not in redis-cache, rebuilding from exchange feed snapshot (<n>ms)'), which is 1-7s of extra work per request. Because request volume was unchanged, that per-request recomputation drove market-data-service CPU from ~45% to ~90-94%, inflating its p99 from ~40ms to ~1.9s. pricing-engine calls market-data-service synchronously and breached its own deadline ('quote computation deadline exceeded: market-data-service took <n>ms'), pushing pricing-engine p99 >2s and api-gateway p99 up to the trading screens. No human-initiated change triggered this: no deployment to pricing-engine/market-data-service/redis-cache/exchange-gateway, and no config change anywhere in the window.

causal_chain.claim: No deployment or config change precedes onset on the quote path (only unrelated auth-service v7.2.0 at 11:30Z, ~110 min earlier); redis-cache has 0 deployments and 0 config changes in the onset window
redis-cache primary redis-cache-2 fails health checks (3 consecutive PING timeouts) at 13:22:10Z; replica redis-cache-3 is promoted at 13:22:52Z with an EMPTY dataset (replica was resyncing) [F34]

The empty-replica promotion empties the shared cache: memory_pct collapses 74.63% -> 6.0% at 13:22Z (consistent with an emptied dataset), connected_clients drops 311.64 -> 40.39 at 13:22Z, and hit_ratio_pct falls 95.9% (13:20Z) -> 10.82% (13:22Z)

market-data-service, a redis-cache consumer, must rebuild quotes from the exchange feed snapshot - the dominant log pattern is 'cache miss storm: quote:<n> not in redis-cache, rebuilding from exchange feed snapshot (<n>ms)', count 37, examples 6864ms / 5018ms

With request_rate flat (967.22 req/s at 13:19Z, 985.77 at 13:21Z, inside the 907-1007 baseline; whole-window mean 951.56, max 1044.69 pre-incident at 12:44Z), the extra work per request is what drives market-data-service CPU from 44.85% (13:20Z) to 90.0% (13:22Z, max 93.99%) and holds ~90% thereafter; memory shows no buildup
The CPU saturation inflates market-data-service latency_p99 from 39-41ms to 1160.98ms avg at 13:20Z, peaking 1910.47ms at 13:25Z

pricing-engine's synchronous call to market-data-service blows its deadline; its only ERROR pattern is 'quote computation deadline exceeded: market-data-service took <n>ms' (192 matched, non-zero downstream durations 1-8.5s)
pricing-engine p99 (>2s) and error_rate (~4%) rise in the same 13:20Z bucket and propagate to api-gateway p99 (up to 2554ms), degrading quotes on trading screens

Scope matches: redis-cache is the only shared:true node, on both pricing-engine's and market-data-service's path, and has cache edges into four consumers; exchange-gateway (market-data-service's other dependency) stayed flat at 127-136ms and thus is not the slow component

redis-cache host CPU is flat (20.34-24.37%) so the fault is not redis host CPU; redis evictions_per_min is flat (1.96-4.13 keys/min) so eviction pressure did not trigger the collapse; the trigger is the node/health failure and empty-replica promotion
Post-failover client reconnect storm (15048 -> 29623 -> 92851 new connections/10s at 13:30-13:40Z) is downstream churn, extending the degradation

assumptions: The market-data-service 'cache miss storm' log and the redis-cache empty-replica promotion describe the same causality (misses are because the promoted primary is empty), rather than two independent coincidences in the same bucket.

The 13:20Z metric-bucket onset versus the 13:22:10Z failover log reflects bucket-boundary/aggregation artifacts only; i.e. the failover is the first discrete event. 4-min bucket resolution cannot prove redis preceded market-data-service within the bucket (F35's 120s resolution does show redis hit-ratio still 95.9% at 13:20Z and collapsing at 13:22Z).

market-data-service has no independent fault of its own; its CPU saturation is attributed to the extra per-request rebuild work (F29/F30 reasoning) since throughput is flat and memory shows no buildup.
Why redis-cache-2 stopped answering PINGs (OOM/host/network) is not captured by any available telemetry; the origin is the redis-cache node failure, whatever its sub-cause.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Load/capacity saturation of market-data-service at a market-open-like traffic surge
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A burst of request volume (market-open-like activity) hit market-data-service, saturating its provisioned CPU capacity (44% -> ~90-94%) without any faulty change, inflating its latency to ~1.9s, which caused pricing-engine's downstream deadline breaches and the trading-screen slowdown. The redis hit-ratio collapse is treated as a consequence of the surge (working-set/churn) rather than an independent cause.

causal_chain.claim: Request volume to market-data-service surges, exceeding provisioned capacity
market-data-service CPU saturates (44.85% at 13:20Z -> 90.0% at 13:22Z, max 93.99%, ~90% thereafter)
market-data-service p99 rises from ~40ms to ~1.16-1.91s in the same 13:20Z bucket
pricing-engine deadline-exceeded errors name market-data-service with 1-8.5s downstream durations
pricing-engine and api-gateway p99 rise in the same bucket, degrading quotes in the app
The redis hit-ratio collapse and the failover to an empty replica are a side effect of the same surge rather than a cause

assumptions: A request_rate spike exists at onset despite the two direct measurements showing none - this is now directly contradicted, so this assumption is treated as falsified rather than merely unqueried.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Its first hop is now directly measured and refuted: market-data-service request_rate is flat at the onset (967.22 req/s at 13:19Z, 985.77 at 13:21Z, inside the 907-1007 baseline; whole-window mean 951.56, max 1044.69 pre-incident at 12:44Z - F25/F26), and a 10% pre-incident blip at 12:44Z caused no degradation while the incident produced ~2x CPU at zero volume increase (F30). Memory shows no buildup (F27) and evictions do not spike (F31). The CPU-with-flat-QPS pattern is instead explained by extra per-request work, which the logs attribute to cache-miss rebuilds (F28/F29), and the discrete empty-replica failover event (F34) supplies a non-load trigger that a capacity surge cannot.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Reporter's implicit suspicion: pricing-engine-internal stall (slow query / GC / pool exhaustion)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: pricing-engine itself stalls internally - a slow query, GC pause, or connection-pool exhaustion - and the deadline-exceeded alerts are its own internal failure rather than a downstream dependency problem.

causal_chain.claim: pricing-engine internal resource exhaustion (GC/memory/pool)

api-gateway and trading screens slow

assumptions: Memory/GC/pool metrics for pricing-engine were never obtained (stated gap), so an internal stall on those specific axes is not fully excluded.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: pricing-engine CPU is flat and unsaturating (34.59-44.48%, F12); its only error text explicitly blames the downstream call to market-data-service (F9); market-data-service latency/CPU (F10/F14/F15), a discrete redis failover to an empty replica (F34) and a cache-miss-storm log signature (F28) all degrade in the same bucket. A pricing-engine-internal stall would not produce matching degradation in market-data-service and redis-cache. The unqueried memory/GC axes do not overturn the explicit downstream attribution.

The 110-minute quiet gap between deploy and onset is coincidence or slow-building.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: auth-service is not on pricing-engine's dependency path (F4); no config change exists in-window (F3) and redis-cache/exchange-gateway/order-service individually show zero deployments and zero config changes (F19-F22); the 110-minute gap between the 11:30Z deploy and the 13:20Z onset (F7/F18) is far too long for a cookie-hardening change. Crucially, the onset now has a concrete redis-internal trigger - redis-cache-2 PING failure and empty-replica promotion at 13:22Z (F34) - which is a complete competing explanation with no auth-service involvement. Redis hit_ratio collapses to 10.82%; memory_pct collapses to 6.0%; connected_clients drops from ~311 to 40.39; market-data-service CPU steps to 90.0%.

Failover: replica redis-cache-3 promoted to primary; dataset on new primary is EMPTY (replica was resyncing).

recommended_actions.action: Immediate mitigation: restore/repopulate the emptied redis-cache keyspace (warm the cache from the exchange feed snapshot / replay the working set) so market-data-service stops rebuilding every quote, then verify redis-cache hit_ratio_pct recovers from the 10-18% band toward the >95% baseline.
recommended_actions.rationale: The hit-ratio collapse from 95.9% to 10.82% caused by promotion of an EMPTY replica is the trigger of the entire chain; restoring cache contents removes the per-request 1-7s rebuild work driving market-data-service CPU to ~90% and pricing-engine deadline breaches.

recommended_actions.action: Immediate mitigation: if failover must be repeated, fail over only to a replica with a non-empty, in-sync dataset (or block promotion of a resyncing replica), preventing a second empty-replica promotion of redis-cache-3 while it resyncs.
recommended_actions.rationale: The empty dataset on the promoted replica is the immediate mechanical cause of the cache-miss storm; a repeat promotion of an unsynced replica would re-trigger the same storm.

recommended_actions.action: Immediate mitigation: shed or rate-limit non-quote load on market-data-service and blunting the client reconnect storm at redis-cache to relieve CPU saturation while the cache warms.
recommended_actions.rationale: market-data-service CPU is pinned at ~90% and redis-cache is logging up to 92851 new connections/10s; reducing load accelerates recovery without touching the failing causal path.

recommended_actions.action: Short term: investigate why redis-cache-2 stopped answering PINGs (OOM, host fault, network) — obtain redis node-level host telemetry, since none exists today.
recommended_actions.rationale: The sub-cause of the primary failure is the true trigger and is undetermined; without it recurrence cannot be prevented and only the consequence (failover) is visible.

recommended_actions.action: Short term: verify post-fix that market-data-service CPU returns to ~45%, its p99 to ~40ms, redis-cache hit_ratio >95%, and pricing-engine p99 back to 55-66ms, and confirm the cache-miss-storm WARN stops.
recommended_actions.rationale: These are the exact signals that degraded together at onset (F7/F10/F14/F15/F28/F35); their recovery confirms the causal chain and closure.

recommended_actions.action: Long term: add redis-cache keyspace_size / used_memory / replication_lag metrics and alert on cache hit_ratio collapse and on promotion of an unsynced (empty) replica.
recommended_actions.rationale: redis-cache currently exposes only five metrics with no keyspace or replication metric (F37), so the empty-dataset premise could only be inferred from memory_pct/clients collapse (F32/F33); direct metrics would detect and prevent recurrence.

recommended_actions.action: Long term: harden the failover/HA policy so a replica that is resyncing cannot be promoted (require data-in-sync check), and review redis-cache-2 health-check sensitivity (3 consecutive PING timeouts).
recommended_actions.rationale: The incident's harm came specifically from promoting an empty, resyncing replica; this matches the HIST-107 precedent ('Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica') and prevents recurrence of a cold-cache storm.

recommended_actions.action: Long term: add a synchronous-call deadline/bulkhead or cache-miss backpressure between pricing-engine and market-data-service so a downstream rebuild storm cannot inflate pricing-engine p99 to trading screens.
recommended_actions.rationale: pricing-engine's deadlines were breached purely by the synchronous downstream call taking 1-8.5s (F9), and the degradation propagated to api-gateway/trading screens (F11); a bound would contain blast radius next time.

data_gaps: No telemetry explains WHY redis-cache-2 stopped answering PINGs (OOM/host/network) — no redis node-level host telemetry was available, so the actual trigger of the primary failure is undetermined.

redis-cache exposes no keyspace_size, used_memory, or replication_lag metric (only memory_pct), so the empty-dataset premise rests on a log line plus inferred memory_pct/connected_clients collapse rather than a direct key-count measurement.

The miss-storm-to-CPU-saturation hop is inferred from co-timing plus log text; there is no independent cache-miss count series, and the market-data-service log result was truncated (total_matched 40, returned 10), so exact miss-storm onset between 13:17:23Z and 13:22:25Z cannot be pinned.
All latency series are 4-min buckets (redis hit_ratio at 120s), so sub-bucket onset ordering among pricing-engine, market-data-service and api-gateway cannot be strictly proven.

pricing-engine memory/GC/restart metrics were never obtained, so a pricing-engine-internal stall on those specific axes is not fully excluded (though contradicted by the explicit downstream attribution and flat CPU).

The first deployment listing was partial (a shard did not respond); a clean retry returned the same single deployment, but a silently missing entry outside the responding shards remains a small residual risk.

A historical search for a non-failover cause of a hit-ratio collapse (eviction policy change, working-set growth) was never completed, so H1 versus an eviction-based variant could not be distinguished from history — though current eviction/memory telemetry argues against an eviction trigger.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that market-data-service request_rate actually spiked at onset (e.g. a volume surge masked by the truncated 2-min buckets) would support H2 load-driven CPU saturation over cache-miss rebuild work.

Evidence that the redis hit-ratio collapse was caused by eviction/maxmemory pressure or working-set churn rather than an emptied dataset (e.g. a keyspace_size drop with memory staying high, or an eviction-policy change) would undermine the empty-replica mechanism.
Discovery of a deployment or config change on pricing-engine, market-data-service, redis-cache, exchange-gateway or order-service preceding 13:20Z would re-open H4 (change-induced degradation).

Evidence that market-data-service degraded before redis-cache (i.e. its CPU/latency rose while hit_ratio was still >95%) would reverse the causality direction, supporting an internal market-data-service fault or upstream surge.
Evidence of a pricing-engine-internal stall (GC pause, memory saturation, connection-pool exhaustion, restarts) coinciding with onset would revive H3.
Demonstration that redis-cache-3 was in fact fully synced (non-empty) at promotion would falsify the empty-replica premise and require a different explanation for the hit-ratio collapse.

pricing-engine cpu_pct shows no saturation during the incident: mean 39.83%, max 44.48%, with the 13:20Z and 13:24Z buckets at 39.06% and 40.88% respectively (range 34.59-44.48% across the whole window, essentially unchanged from pre-incident). This argues against CPU saturation as the pricing-engine-side cause.

redis-cache hit_ratio_pct collapses at the same 13:20Z bucket as the incident onset: it was stable at 95.5-96.14% through 13:15Z, then dropped to avg 45.09% in the 13:20Z bucket (max 96.34, i.e. within-bucket transition) and 13.04% at 13:25Z, staying low (~13-48%) for the rest of the window. redis-cache is the only shared dependency on both pricing-engine's and market-data-service's path.

market-data-service CPU saturates in the same onset bucket: cpu_pct was flat at 43-47% through 13:15Z, then jumped to avg 72.72% (max 93.99%) in the 13:20Z 5-min bucket; zoomed to 2-min buckets the step is between 13:20Z (44.85%) and 13:22Z (90.0%, max 93.99%), then ~90% for the rest of the window. This is the only component on the dependency path showing resource saturation at onset.

market-data-service latency_p99_ms jumps in the same 13:20Z bucket: 39-41ms through 13:15Z, then avg 1160.98ms (max 1979.98ms) at 13:20Z, peaking 1910.47ms at 13:25Z. Onset is concurrent with (not lagging) pricing-engine's latency/error jump, consistent with market-data-service being the slow callee named in the pricing-engine deadline errors.

exchange-gateway (the other dependency of market-data-service) does NOT show latency degradation: p99 was ~127-136ms across the entire window including onset, with min 114.0 / max 143.91 and mean 130.29, i.e. flat through 13:20Z and beyond. Its scope does not match the blast radius, ruling it out as the slow component.

redis-cache's own CPU shows no saturation: cpu_pct held 20.34-24.37% (mean 22.02%) across the whole window including the 13:20Z bucket (21.61%), so the cache hit-ratio collapse is not explained by cache host CPU exhaustion at the observed resolution.

Onset ordering is redis-cache hit_ratio collapse + market-data-service CPU saturation + market-data-service latency + pricing-engine latency/errors all first appearing in the 13:20Z bucket, with no preceding deployment (only unrelated auth-service v7.2.0 at 11:30Z) or config change. Therefore no change-history item times before the latency onset; the shared-component (redis-cache) and its consumer market-data-service are the only candidates whose scope (shared dependency used by both ailing services) and timing match the blast radius.
Redis-cache-scoped change history is empty in the incident window: get_deployments for redis-cache (13:00Z–13:30Z) returned count 0, no deployments, partial:false.
Narrow-scope config check directly around the onset (13:00Z–13:30Z, all services) returned zero config changes, partial:false — no maxmemory-policy change or config reload in the onset window.

exchange-gateway individually returned zero config changes for 12:30Z–14:59Z (partial:false) and zero deployments for the same window — the residual gap that exchange-gateway was never separately checked is now closed.
order-service individually returned zero config changes for 12:30Z–14:59Z (partial:false) and zero deployments for the same window, closing the second part of the residual gap.

redis-cache is confirmed shared:true (type 'redis', owner 'platform') with cache edges into four consumers — auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service — so its hit-ratio collapse can affect both ailing services simultaneously.

The only historical redis failover precedent is HIST-107 (2025-12-09) 'Cold cache storm after redis failover', root cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica'; the tool labels these as leads, and no corresponding promotion/failover event was found in this incident's change history.

refs.quote: "Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica"

findings.statement: market-data-service request_rate is flat across the 13:20Z onset, not spiked: the 2-min buckets 13:19Z=967.22, 13:21Z=985.77 req/s sit inside the pre-incident range. Compare with the 12:00-13:10Z baseline where values run 907-986 req/s and the 13:11Z peak is 1007.79 / max 1025.69 req/s. No step change at onset.

Whole-window request_rate for market-data-service is statistically flat: summary over 12:00-13:34Z is min 878.88, max 1044.69, mean 951.56 req/s (96 points, missing_points 0, partial false). The window max (1044.69) is only ~10% above the mean and occurs pre-incident in the 12:44Z bucket, i.e. the incident contains no exceptional throughput.

market-data-service memory_pct shows no rise at onset and no trend: 13:20Z avg 61.87 (max 65.03), 13:22Z avg 58.8, 13:24Z avg 62.01, versus a 12:00-13:10Z baseline of 58.77-65.79. Full-window summary min 56.87, max 67.82, mean 62.12, comparable to baseline. No memory buildup consistent with a growing queue or sustained load surge.

market-data-service logs explicitly name the mechanism: WARN pattern 'cache miss storm: quote:<n> not in redis-cache, rebuilding from exchange feed snapshot (<n>ms)' is the dominant pattern, count 37, first_seen 13:22:25Z. Example entries: 13:22:25Z quote:84685 rebuilt in 6864ms; 13:25:04Z quote:58862 in 5018ms; the only non-WARN entries in the window are 3 INFO lines (health check, scheduled job heartbeat, batch served).

findings.statement: The CPU step and the cache-miss-storm logs begin at essentially the same time while throughput is unchanged (CPU: 44.85% at 13:20Z -> 90.0% at 13:22Z per F14; misses logged from 13:22:25Z; request_rate 967.22 req/s at 13:19Z and 985.77 at 13:21Z, inside baseline range). Higher CPU at flat QPS therefore reflects more work per request, and the logs attribute that work to redis-cache misses with per-quote rebuilds taking 1-7 seconds.

refs.quote: cache miss storm: quote:58180 not in redis-cache, rebuilding from exchange feed snapshot (2494ms)

findings.statement: This flat-volume + CPU-saturation pattern is inconsistent with H2 (capacity saturation from a load/traffic surge): a 10% one-off request_rate blip occurred pre-incident at 12:44Z (1026.31 req/s) with no degradation, whereas the incident produced a ~2x CPU increase with zero volume increase. It is consistent with H1 (extra per-request work from cache-miss recomputation) as far as market-data-service's own throughput and memory signals can show.

redis-cache evictions_per_min shows no spike at 13:16-13:20Z: it is flat across the whole 13:10-13:30Z window, range 1.96-4.13 keys/min (mean 3.11), with 13:16Z=2.27, 13:17Z=3.56, 13:18Z=2.15, 13:19Z=4.05, 13:20Z=3.52. Eviction is NOT the trigger.

redis-cache memory_pct shows no high-pressure spike before onset: it oscillates 65-75% through 13:21Z (13:20Z=68.09, 13:21Z=74.63) and then COLLAPSES to 6.0% at 13:22Z, staying 6.0-8.69% thereafter. Memory did not max out; the drop is consistent with an emptied/reset dataset rather than memory pressure.

redis-cache connected_clients is steady ~288-332 through 13:21Z (13:20Z=314.11, 13:21Z=311.64), then drops to 40.39 at 13:22Z (37-43 through 13:25Z) before recovering to ~303-313 from 13:26Z onward. The drop coincides exactly with the 13:22Z failover.

redis-cache logs record an internal primary failure and failover: ERROR at 13:22:10Z 'node redis-cache-2 failed health check (3 consecutive PING timeouts); marking primary as down', then WARN at 13:22:52Z 'failover: promoting replica redis-cache-3 to primary; dataset on new primary is empty (replica was resyncing)', and a full resync WARN at 13:28:42Z. This is the redis-internal trigger of the hit-ratio collapse.

findings.statement: redis-cache hit_ratio_pct at finer (120s) resolution: stable 94.72-96.97% through 13:20Z (13:20Z=95.9), then falls to 10.82% at 13:22Z and stays 10.45-18.34% through 13:40Z. The collapse begins in the 13:22Z bucket, aligning with the 13:22Z failover/empty-replica promotion rather than 13:16-13:20Z.

After the failover, redis-cache logs a client reconnect storm: WARN 'client reconnect storm: 15048 new connections in 10s' at 13:30:20Z, escalating to '29623 new connections in 10s' at 13:35:30Z and '92851 new connections in 10s' at 13:40:15Z. This is downstream client (re)connection churn, not an access-pattern change preceding the fault.

client reconnect storm: 92851 new connections in 10s

findings.statement: redis-cache exposes only five metrics: connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct. There is no keyspace_size / used_memory / replication-lag metric available, so keyspace size could not be measured directly (only inferred from the memory_pct and connected_clients collapse).
